entries.clue: Tree resins in health facilities sent back (4)

indicatorNotes.sent back: Something sent back travels the way it came, and an across entry read the way it came runs from its right-hand end.

blocks.note: places people go to be steamed, soaked and massaged are spas, and this entry runs across, so those four letters are read from the far end back

annotation.surface: Tree resin delivered to a chain of health clubs and returned to sender.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the signal for letters hiding inside the clue's own words, and it is joinery — nothing is concealed here, something is turned round. The surface has a delivery going back where it came from, which keeps the last two words looking like part of the story.
annotation.definitionFit: Sap is the fluid a tree runs on, and the sticky resins that bleed from a cut trunk are the stuff the plural names.

entries.clue: Miss embraced by oiled nudist hunk (4,6)

indicatorNotes.oiled: Oiled is British slang for drunk — well oiled — and a drunk's letters will not stay standing in the order they were handed.
indicatorNotes.embraced by: What is embraced by something has that something closing round it from both sides.

blocks.note: the six letters of the sunbather, reset into this order so that a gap opens in the middle
to muff a catch is to miss it, fumbling what should have been held

annotation.surface: An oiled nudist on a beach with a young woman in their arms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Miss' is a verb, not a young woman: to muff something is to miss it. 'Oiled' has to be read as drunk before it will shuffle anything, and the surface works hard to keep it literal.
annotation.definitionFit: Hunk is admiring slang for a powerfully built, good-looking man, which is what the answer calls one too, with more teasing in it.

entries.clue: Race car, for example – or kayak! (10)

annotation.definition: Race car, for example – or kayak!

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a vehicle built for the track, offered as one instance of a class of thing
the reading the setter means: set the second example beside the first and what the two share is not what they are but how they are spelt

annotation.surface: Naming things you might travel in: a car built for the track, or else a small boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For example' is doing honest work — both things named really are instances, just not of any class of vehicle. The word being defined is the one thing in the clue that does not read the same backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A palindrome is a word or phrase spelt the same read either way, and both the car and the boat the clue names qualify once the space comes out.

entries.clue: Common insects: audience hurries away (10)

blocks.note: the people out front at a theatre are the house — a full house, playing to the house
somebody who hurries off flies out of the door

annotation.surface: A theatre audience getting up and leaving in a hurry.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves come from the same building: in a theatre the house is the seating out front and the flies are the space above the stage where scenery is hoisted out of sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Houseflies are the ordinary grey flies that get indoors everywhere in summer, so 'common insects' names them by how unremarkable they are.

entries.clue: Job available in Gap (7)

blocks.note: a post nobody is filling, the thing advertised when a firm is hiring
a space where something has been left out, in a hedge, a wall or a timetable

annotation.surface: A vacancy going at the clothes shop.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital G turns a plain noun into the high-street clothing chain, and that is the whole of the misdirection. The two senses stay close cousins: a post nobody fills is a hole in the staff list.
annotation.definitionFit: An opening is a vacancy — an opening in sales — and also a gap: a hole in a hedge, or one in the day's timetable.

entries.clue: Creep showing how to describe what’s average in two words? (2-3-2)

blocks.note: a middling meal or a middling day is so-so, and this is the front half of that pair
prise that hyphenated pair apart into two separate words and a joiner is needed between them
the back half of the same pair, unchanged

annotation.surface: A creep giving a lesson in how to call something middling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In two words' is not an enumeration of the answer but an instruction to unpack a hyphenated phrase. So-and-so doubles as the polite stand-in for a name nobody wants to say, which is where the insult grew from.
annotation.definitionFit: A so-and-so is what you call someone you think badly of when you are not going to say the real word, and creep is that judgement made plainly.

entries.clue: Egg on this: santé! (6,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is an instruction rather than a synonym: do what it says to a slice of bread — soak it in beaten egg and fry it — and the dish is what you are left with.

blocks.note: the word set in italics is not English, and the language it belongs to is the first half
santé means health, and it is what is said over raised glasses — a salute drunk to somebody

annotation.surface: Urging somebody on, then drinking their health in French.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Egg on' wants to be the phrasal verb meaning to urge, and the egg turns out to be literal. Santé is what the French say as the glasses go up, the job 'cheers' does in English.
annotation.definitionFit: French toast is bread soaked in beaten egg and fried, so the dish is made by doing exactly what the definition instructs.

entries.clue: Notion, almost perfect (4)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost means falling just short, so the word it governs is written out all but its last letter.

blocks.note: a perfect day or a perfect answer is an ideal one
the L standing at the end of that word is the letter left off

annotation.surface: Faint praise for a thought that is nearly, but not quite, faultless.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma does the hiding: 'almost perfect' reads as one verdict and only comes apart into an instruction once you stop trusting it. The italics on 'almost' are the paper's emphasis and carry no wordplay at all.
annotation.definitionFit: An idea and a notion are the same thing — something that has come into your head — with notion carrying a little more of the half-formed about it.

entries.clue: Scandalous author – disturbing eroticist, principally? (4)

indicatorNotes.principally: What comes principally comes first, so each word of the description gives up the letter it opens on and nothing more.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the first word
the letter this noun begins with
the opening letter of the adjective after the dash
the front letter of the last word in the list

annotation.surface: A writer with a scandalous reputation, mainly for unsettling erotica.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs at once — describing the man and handing over its first letter — so nothing is left over to serve as a separate definition. The Marquis de Sade wrote in and out of French prisons and gave his name to sadism.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes the Marquis de Sade, the aristocrat whose erotic novels scandalised France and whose name became a word for cruelty.

entries.clue: What’s in jug? Lichee fruit (4)

indicatorNotes.What’s in: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the letters wanted are already sitting inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: four letters in a row starting at the second, running over the question mark and the space

annotation.surface: Somebody asking what the jug is full of and being told it is lychee.
annotation.walkthrough: The older lichee spelling is there to make the join invisible, and the question mark between the two words is a wall the letters walk straight through. Everyman leans on this device once or twice a puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: The ugli is a citrus fruit, the knobbly green-skinned Jamaican cross between grapefruit and tangerine sold under that trade name.

entries.clue: Messed around with ease, I might be on a roll (6,4)

annotation.definition: I might be on a roll
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a riddle in the first person rather than a synonym: the answer speaks for itself, saying where you would find it.

indicatorNotes.around: To move something around is to shift it from where it sat, and letters shifted about come back in a different order.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
four more letters of fodder, taking the count to ten

annotation.surface: Somebody who fooled about effortlessly and is now having a run of luck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Messed around' looks like one phrase and is two jobs: the first word is the letters and the second is the instruction. 'On a roll' is the second trap — a bread roll, not a winning streak.
annotation.definitionFit: A sesame seed is one of the pale seeds scattered over a burger bun, so the answer really might be found sitting on a roll.

entries.clue: Bureaucrat to avoid waterfowl (8,4)

blocks.note: a senior civil servant in Whitehall is a mandarin, the word borrowed from the scholar-officials of imperial China
to avoid a question or a blow is to duck it

annotation.surface: A civil servant under orders to steer clear of the birds on the pond.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the name arrive by the same route: the bird is east Asian, and its drake was called mandarin for plumage as ornate as a court official's robes. A colony has lived wild in Britain for a century.
annotation.definitionFit: Waterfowl covers the ducks, geese and swans that live on water, and the answer names one of the most ornamental ducks of the lot.

entries.clue: Characters seen in Britain’s Got Talent and The Winter’s Tale? (11)

annotation.definition: Characters seen in Britain’s Got Talent and The Winter’s Tale?

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: the people who appear — the acts on the talent show, the shepherds and kings of the play

blocks.clueFragment: Britain’s Got Talent and The Winter’s Tale?
blocks.note: the reading the setter means: look at the two titles as printed, and the mark each carries in its first word is the thing being asked for

annotation.surface: The people who turn up on a Saturday-night talent show and in a Shakespeare play.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' means both a person in a story and a mark on the page, and only the second survives a look at the printed titles. Britain's Got Talent is ITV's Saturday-night variety contest; The Winter's Tale is Shakespeare's late romance.
annotation.definitionFit: An apostrophe is a typographic character, and each title carries one in a possessive, so the clue's two examples are meant literally.

entries.clue: Rising gyration (10)

blocks.note: a revolt — the people of a country coming out against those who rule them
one full turn about an axis, the way a wheel or a planet goes round

annotation.surface: A turning movement that climbs as it goes.
annotation.walkthrough: Two nouns side by side, each a complete definition, with nothing to say which is which — the shortest kind of clue and often the slowest to fall. The French and Russian sense is the first; the earth's yearly circuit of the sun is the second.
annotation.definitionFit: A revolution is a rising against a government, and it is also one complete turn — an engine's revs are the same word shortened.

entries.clue: Alternative adopted by disruptive shakeout somewhere on the Yellow Sea (5,5)

indicatorNotes.disruptive: Something disruptive breaks up the arrangement it finds, so the letters it is applied to will not come back in their old order.
indicatorNotes.adopted by: A child adopted by a family is taken right into it, so the piece named goes inside rather than alongside.

blocks.note: the eight letters of the word, reset into this order so that a gap opens near the end
the little word that offers a choice between one thing and another

annotation.surface: A disruptive round of job cuts at a firm that takes on the alternative offered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Alternative' as two letters is worth banking — the word that offers a choice turns up constantly. The Yellow Sea has China on one side and both Koreas on the other, so the definition alone will not pick a country; the letters do that.
annotation.definitionFit: South Korea's west coast is the eastern shore of the Yellow Sea, so the country is one of the places the definition could be pointing at.

entries.clue: Pine marten perhaps leading in distance raced (7)

indicatorNotes.leading: What leads goes in front, so the piece it is attached to is written before the other one.

blocks.note: the marten is one of the animals trapped for its coat, and 'perhaps' marks it as an example of the stuff rather than the word for it
to pine for something is to long for it

annotation.surface: A pine marten out in front over a racing distance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pine marten' is one animal in the surface and two separate pieces underneath, which is the whole of the difficulty. A furlong is an eighth of a mile, 220 yards, and British horse races are still measured in them.
annotation.definitionFit: A furlong is the unit British racing measures its courses in, so 'distance raced' names it by the one place the old measure is still used.

entries.clue: Ignoring some affront, he got busy (2-3-2)

indicatorNotes.Ignoring some: Ignoring some of what is written means keeping only part of it, and the part kept here is an unbroken run of letters.

blocks.note: seven letters in a row beginning at the fifth letter of the first word, crossing a comma and two spaces

annotation.surface: A man who let an insult pass and threw himself into his work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ignoring' looks like an order to drop something, and nothing is dropped — it is the setter's way of saying that only part of what follows counts. The letters run straight through the comma, which is where the eye stops.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody on the go is never still, out and about from morning to night, which is the plain everyday sense of busy.

entries.clue: Everyman initially nags deputies: they fill the cells (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description rather than a synonym — 'the ones who fill the cells' — with the pronoun standing in for the plural answer.

indicatorNotes.initially: What is done initially is done first, so the word it governs gives up only the letter standing at its front.

blocks.note: this puzzle is signed Everyman, so the name stands for the one doing the writing
the letter this verb begins with
a ship's mate is the officer who stands in for the captain, and the plural is the deputies of the clue

annotation.surface: The setter opening proceedings by nagging the deputies.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman means I whenever this setter writes it, the same way other setters put themselves into their own clues. 'Cells' wants to be a biology lesson or a phone network and is a prison landing.
annotation.definitionFit: Inmates are the people held in a prison, so the cells they fill are the locked ones off a landing rather than anything under a microscope.

entries.clue: Attacking footballer, one with brilliant match? (7)

blocks.note: the forward whose job is to get on the end of crosses and score
read the other way: somebody holding a matchstick they have just set alight

annotation.surface: A forward who had an outstanding game.
annotation.walkthrough: In the surface a brilliant match is an outstanding game; in the second definition it is a matchstick giving off light. Football's striker is the player furthest forward, the club's designated scorer.
annotation.definitionFit: A striker is the forward a football team looks to for its goals, and anyone who strikes a match is a striker of it, the brilliance being the flame.

entries.clue: Corroborate order for Paddington to go? (4,3)

blocks.note: Paddington is the marmalade-eating bear of Michael Bond's children's books, named after the London station where the Browns find him
the one-word order that tells somebody to leave

annotation.surface: Backing up an instruction that Paddington should leave.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark owns the joke — nobody barks an order at Paddington — and it is also the only sign that the second half of the clue has stopped meaning what it says. As an order, that second word needs no verb with it.
annotation.definitionFit: To bear out a claim is to back it up with evidence, which is what corroborate asks for in a courtroom or a report.

entries.clue: Read aloud Howl, poem: will it scan? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a question rather than a synonym: the thing is identified by what it is for, which is to be scanned.

indicatorNotes.Read aloud: Reading something aloud turns it into a sound, and what is wanted is another way of spelling that same sound.

blocks.note: a dog's howl is a bark, and said aloud the k at its end can be written with a c
a poem, particularly one addressed to something in praise of it, is an ode

annotation.surface: Somebody asking whether Ginsberg's Howl has a regular metre.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scan' is the verse sense in the surface — whether a poem's metre is regular — and the checkout sense in the definition. The split the wordplay wants falls in a place the word itself would never break.
annotation.definitionFit: A barcode exists to be read by a scanner at a till, so asking whether it will scan is asking the only question anybody ever asks of one.

entries.clue: Writhing, hurt, rocks or reels at first, filled with dread (6-6)

indicatorNotes.Writhing: Something writhing is twisting about, and letters twisting about do not stay in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.at first: What comes at first is the letter a word opens on, so only that one is taken from it.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder
the letter the word reels begins with, the twelfth

annotation.surface: Somebody hurt and writhing, rocking or reeling, and frightened out of their wits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rocks or reels' reads as one pair of verbs and is split down the middle: two of the three words are letters and only the front of the third is taken. Nothing in the surface separates them.
annotation.definitionFit: Being horror-struck is dread arriving all at once and stopping you where you stand, so 'filled with dread' catches the state if not the suddenness.

entries.clue: Piece of info, ASAP! (4)

blocks.note: one figure lifted out of a set of numbers, the kind quoted at half-time
the word shouted in hospital dramas when something is wanted this minute

annotation.surface: Somebody demanding a figure and demanding it immediately.
annotation.walkthrough: The urgent sense comes from the Latin statim, at once, and reaches most people through hospital dramas rather than hospitals. The other sense is the newsroom and dressing-room short form of statistic.
annotation.definitionFit: A stat is a statistic, one figure pulled out of the data, and 'stat!' is the doctor's order for something to be done without delay.

entries.clue: Look furtively – in both directions? (4)

indicatorNotes.in both directions?: A word that works in both directions reads the same from either end, so there is nothing to turn round — only the symmetry to notice.

blocks.note: the definition end of the clue: a quick glance taken when you should not be looking at all
the wordplay end: four letters that come out the same read either way, which is all the help given

annotation.surface: Sneaking a glance one way and then the other.
annotation.walkthrough: Reading the same either way is the whole of the wordplay, so no fragment here hands over letters. The surface has somebody checking left and right, which is what the instruction is pretending to describe.
annotation.definitionFit: To peep is to look quickly and secretly — through a curtain, round a door — and the furtiveness is the part that separates it from a plain look.

entries.clue: According to Spooner, not one youngster or the other is to wed (3,3,4)

indicatorNotes.According to Spooner: The Reverend Spooner's trademark slip was to exchange the opening sounds of two words as he said them, so the pair named here trade their fronts.

blocks.clueFragment: not one youngster or the other
blocks.note: 'not one … or the other' is neither; hand its opening n to the other word, take a t back, and what is left is two short words
a youngster is a tot; give it the n it has just been handed and the ordinary spelling of that sound puts a silent k out in front

annotation.surface: Spooner reporting that neither of the two children is to be married.
annotation.walkthrough: Say 'neither tot' aloud and trade the noises at the front: neither is nigh-ther in British speech, so with a t on it the sound comes out as two small words. The second half hides an unsounded k.
annotation.definitionFit: To tie the knot is the everyday idiom for getting married, the knot being the bond the couple are said to be making.

entries.clue: In den, with stomach churning, peddler of falsehoods (4)

indicatorNotes.stomach churning: A churning stomach is one being turned over and over, and letters turned over like that settle in a new order.

blocks.note: a wild animal's den is its lair, and those four letters are the ones churned

annotation.surface: Sitting in a den with your stomach turning over.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters shuffled are not written in the clue: den has to be turned into its four-letter synonym before anything can be rearranged, a step beyond what most anagrams ask. Of the arrangements that make words, only one names a person.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody who tells lies is a liar, and calling them a peddler of falsehoods casts the lying as a trade they deal in.

entries.clue: Records rugby highlights in woven illustrations (10)

blocks.note: to record a programme is to tape it, and these are the things it is recorded on
a try is rugby's five-point score, made by grounding the ball behind the opposition's line, and the high point of any move

annotation.surface: Filming the best moments of a rugby match.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Records' is a verb in the surface and a plural noun underneath, which is the whole of the misdirection. The Bayeux Tapestry is the famous one, and it is embroidery rather than weaving.
annotation.definitionFit: A tapestry is a picture made by weaving coloured threads into the cloth itself, so the definition says both what they show and how they are made.

entries.clue: Empire invaded by Spanish finding home by Central America (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The word names the people and their ruler rather than the empire itself, though 'the Inca' is regularly used for the empire they built.

blocks.note: somebody at home is in, as in asking whether she is in
the two-letter short form of Central America, the isthmus running from Guatemala down to Panama

annotation.surface: An empire overrun by Spaniards who had made their home next to Central America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Invaded by' looks like an instruction to put one thing inside another and is history instead. The empire's heartland was the Andes, which is South America — the Central America of the clue is only letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The Inca empire ran down the Andes from Ecuador to Chile until Pizarro's expedition brought it down in the 1530s, so naming the invader picks out which empire is meant.
